Copper Quarterly Report April 2009 # Executive Summary Diversion from reality CRU estimates that global demand slumped by 18% year-on-year in Q1 2009, a clear indicator that we are in the middle of the worst economic crisis since the early 1970s. Despite the collapse in demand, production declined by only 4.5% resulting in a market surplus in the quarter of 513,000t. Looking forward, CRU believes that global demand for copper is on course to decline by 13.1% to 15.4Mt this year. Excluding China, we estimate that consumption will register a 19% collapse this year. China remains crucial in terms of growth and we expect demand here to expand by 3%. If, as CRU expects, there is also a 900,000t curtailment in refined production during H2 2009 due to low prices and a raw material (concentrate) shortfall, we expect the global surplus to increase to 1.3Mt this year from 427,000t in 2008. However, it is important to note that these curtailments will only occur if production becomes unprofitable. This need to curtail output that is currently operating on a profitable basis drives our price forecast for the remainder of 2009. Given the higher than forecast prices for Q1 2009, we have revised our price forecast for 2009 upwards to $1.55/lb. Despite the clear, gloomy, fundamental picture above, prices continued to rally throughout Q1 2009 and are currently trading in the region of $4,500/t. The market should consider and plan for a scenario dominated by collapsing global demand, based upon the reality of Q4 2008 and Q1 2009. Instead, many appear to find this too disastrous to contemplate and prefer to be diverted from reality and focus on the hope that, short-term, China will limit the downside. The sharp rise in Chinese imports adds further fuel to the view that the SRB have been in the market. We estimate that Chinese apparent consumption of cathode rose by a stunning 31% in Q1. Data: CRU|ported Refin|ed Copper|Stocks inclu|de unreport|ed stock ch|ange as at|end of perio|d|| The other significant factors accounting for the rise in Chinese refined imports are: - SRB buying, which we estimate accounts for up to 100,000t of the rise in imports in Q1 2009. - 20,000t from SHFE-LME arbitrage positions. - 100,000t from one-off restocking, which began following the Lunar New Year in February and has gathered momentum in anticipation of higher economic activity in H2 2009. - The extra liquidity from the easing of monetary policy has translated into higher asset prices across the board, including those of steel, iron ore and more recently real estate. ### Once Chinese buying abates, prices will be weighed down by a 1Mt surplus On a purely fundamental basis, copper should not be trading at $5,000/t. Global demand fell by an estimated 18% year-on-year in Q1 2009 and production fell by only 4.5%, resulting in a market surplus of 513,000t during the quarter. This build up was initially reflected in the rise in exchange stocks of over 200,000t during the first two months of the year. However, the pick up in Chinese buying and the sustained positive SHFE-LME arbitrage saw this rise in stocks halted and reversed in March and into April. With SRB buying accounting for an estimated 100,000t, even adjusting the market surplus for this unavailable material takes the Q1 balance down to “only” 413,000t. We expect that the seasonal pattern of Chinese imports seen over the past two years, in which Q1 is the strongest quarter and Q3 the weakest, will emerge again this year. Once that happens, this could be the trigger for prices to retreat and exchange stocks to trend higher. We now expect prices to hit a quarterly average low of $1.20/lb in Q4 and average $1.55/lb for the year as a whole, which is up by 20¢/lb when compared to our $1.25/lb forecast in the January Quarterly. The renewed downward pressure on prices will prompt a reversal of supply-side restarts and generate further production cutbacks. Total refined production this year will therefore fall by 8.0% to 16.7Mt, or marginally higher than in 2005, and contain the market surplus this year to about 1.3Mt, or almost 1Mt when the estimated 300,000t of SRB stock build is discounted. CRU International Limited confidential 4 Copper Quarterly Report April 2009 Executive Summary Refined copper demand will only bounce back in 2010 due mainly to restocking throughout the supply chain following the shock to the system that began in Q4 2008. With prices averaging $1.35/lb, refined production growth will be just 1.2% next year and the market surplus will be trimmed to 190,000t. Prices should begin to revive in 2011, as the full impact of government stimulus packages is felt. Productio

n growth will begin to recover in 2011 by which time we expect the market will be broadly in balance. Demand growth should remain above trend through to 2013, but production growth is forecast to fail to keep pace, as disruptions and the collective underperformance in the mining sector seen during the boom years continue to constrain overall refined production growth to an average of 4.4%. As a result the market will move into deficit in 2012 and 2013 and prices will begin to rise, averaging $2/lb in 2012 and $2.40/lb in 2013. ### China pulls further away The demand picture is one of a divergence between China and the rest of the world. We estimate that Chinese consumption of refined copper will rise by 3.0% this year. This fairly rosy picture for China will be more than offset by the catastrophic decline in demand in the rest of the world. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report April 2009 Executive Summary 5 The picture in developed markets is difficult to paint as anything other than dire. In the US, manufacturing activity has contracted rapidly for 14 months in a row. Japan’s copper demand is expected to shrink by nearly a third in 2009, as it suffers from its heavy dependence on exports. Western European manufacturing activity is still very weak, down by 13% year-on-year in March. In addition, the availability of credit globally has yet to improve significantly, hampering financing of new projects and working capital. It is also unlikely that government stimulus packages in these countries will have a positive impact on copper demand until the end of 2009. Eastern Europe is faring a little better, with wirerod exports remaining relatively strong and cushioning the downturn in domestic demand. an minimal cutbacks and restarts, for now The January Quarterly supply outlook highlighted mine cutbacks and project delays. According to the latest available information, announced mine production cutbacks and closures for 2009 amount to a total of 696,000t of copper, of which two-thirds will be copper in concentrates and one-third will be EW copper cathode. Since the previous Quarterly there have been over 280,000t of new mine cutbacks, with most announced in late January, after the Quarterly had been completed. Since then, cutback activity has shifted to smelters and refineries. The majority of smelting/refining cutbacks have been demand-led, as integrated smelters/refineries, especially in Asia, cut back by 10-20% on their planned production this year in the face of falling demand for copper and by-product sulphuric acid. Smelters and refineries have announced total reductions of just under 640,000t for this year as indicated in the table below, which is almost 390,000t higher than has been included in the January Quarterly. Sulphuric acid itself has been a reason for some cutbacks and may become more important going forward. The sulphuric acid market moved into surplus in the final quarter of 2008 as production of acid from base metal smelting continued to grow while demand from the fertiliser industry, which accounts for around half of acid demand, fell. Acid prices have fallen sharply and some smelters have had difficulty placing all of their acid with customers. We understand that some Chinese smelters have had to pay to have their acid disposed of, while net acid revenue is negative for smelters in other regions, as transportation costs exceed delivered prices. As storage capacity becomes full, the threat of production cutbacks looms. As yet, only two cutbacks have been announced as a direct result of the oversupply of acid, that at Boliden’s operations in the first quarter and that at Xstrata’s Kidd Creek smelter in the second quarter. |Announced s

### Will prices drive supply cutbacks later this year? In the January Quarterly we highlighted the supply cutbacks and project delays that were announced in Q4 2008 and anticipated that there would be more to come through. However, with the price well above the cost of production for most mines so far this year, and despite the looming surplus, the anticipated response has been muted. The mine cutbacks for 2009 as a whole that have been announced since Q4 2008 in response to the collapse in the copper price and by- and co-product prices amounts to 696,000t. However, with the price trading at around $4,500/t the first restarts have been announced. Given the poor outlook for global demand as outlined above, and the fact that Chinese buying will eventually slow later this year, we remain bearish on the price outlook given our market balance. For many companies, high debt levels are currently a major problem, putting pressure on copper mines to maintain production and cash flow in order to meet their short run commitments and to try to improve their long term capital structure. Furthermore, a diversified mining company will base its curtailment decisions on the profitability of each asset within their portfolio, and to such a company, a relatively marginal copper operation may still be valuable compared to its other assets, and make closure even less likely. In the main, however, the lack of further curtailments is due to the fact that the copper price has rebounded to levels at which most copper mines are able to make a profit, based on our assessment of copper mine costs. As the following chart indicates, we believe that the average 2009 business costs of mines in each region are well below the H1 2009 price level. However, CRU expects copper prices to fall in H2 2009 to below the average costs in both Europe and North America, and far closer to the averages in the other regions. In th

is situation, which mines are most at risk of curtailments or closures should prices fall as we forecast? The main mining assets at risk fall into five categories: CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report April 2009 Executive Summary 9 - **SXEW operations** had on average 24% higher costs than concentrates mines in 2008 and will remain higher for the next five years. - **Copper-moly and copper-cobalt mines** should remain high-cost and subject to closure before other operations, as the price of neither moly nor cobalt is expected to recover significantly over the outlook period - **European** , **North America** and **Chinese mines** all are relatively high cost regions. - **Mining companies with high debt levels** will find it difficult and more expensive to refinance debt when it needs to be rolled over. - **Mining companies that have hedged** may find that when their current hedges expire, they face a fall in revenues, especially if this occurs in H2 of 2009 and 2010. Whilst amongst the smelting/refining operations: - **European and North American operations** will be the most vulnerable to lower prices and weak copper demand as they are facing the biggest drop in demand in their regional markets. - **The global oversupply of sulphuric acid** could potentially affect smelters in all regions. However, we believe that those in North America are most at risk. - **Chinese smelters** are particularly vulnerable to shortfalls in the availability of concentrates and scrap. Custom smelters elsewhere are covered with long term contracts for concentrates and also have well established sources for scrap. - **New smelting and refining capacity in China** will face difficulty securing sufficient raw materials. 2009 CRU’s LME copper cash price: US$3,417/t

CRU International Limited confidential 10 Copper Quarterly Report April 2009 Executive Summary ### Points to watch #### **These are the main demand factors to be watched:** - We may have underestimated the effect of scrap on refined demand. In our current demand outlook we estimate that globally there will be a 500,000t benefit to refined consumption in 2009 due to the shortage of scrap. Over and above the lack of scrap in the market, we believe that the “distrust” implications could support higher demand for refined cathode, possibility as high as 700,000t, particularly in China and India which consume the highest proportion of scrap within the semis sector. - The higher prevailing prices could see more scrap made available to the market in the short term. However, it is likely to be consumed locally rather than exported, as merchants are likely to be far more risk averse. - The economic downturn may prove longer and more severe than in our base case. Credit tig

htness, deflation and protectionism are all factors which could constrain demand further in the short term and result in a longer than anticipated downturn. 



- China remains an enigma.  Industrial production growth of 5.1% in the first quarter is at odds with the 8.5% year-on-year decline in industrial electricity consumption.  Even if we have double refined copper demand growth this year, i.e. 6% rather than our current forecast of 3%, this would only add an additional 150,000t to Chinese consumption and would reduce the market surplus by a similar amount. 



- There are now theories circulating that the Chinese government is building up inventory of a broad basket of commodities as part of a plan to diversify their $1.95 trillion foreign exchange reserves away from US dollars.  That may be the case, given that the Governor of the Central Bank floated the idea of establishing a new international reserve currency anchored in a broad basket of commodities, such as the one originally proposed by Keynes in the gold standard era to diversify exchange rates away from just one commodity. However, the factors noted earlier in this Executive Summary easily account for all of the increase in imports so far, without reverting to any fundamental change in Chinese macroeconomic policy. 



- If copper prices go higher at a time of credit restriction, this could inhibit consumers’ ability to buy more units and further delay the recovery. 

#### **These are the main mining factors to be considered:** 



- Mine operating cost inflation is other than expected.  Higher costs would cause more closures and an overestimation of our production forecast.  Stagnated costs would discourage cutbacks and present a risk of underestimation to the production forecast. 



- The price of a variety of different commodities could affect our production forecasts.  A collapse in gold prices would lead to closure of Cu-Au and Au-Cu mines and an underestimate of production.  A spike in oil prices due to geopolitical events would force more mines to cutback/close.  Prolonged low sulphuric acid prices would discourage SXEW mines to cutback, but would force more smelters to cutback.  An upturn in steel demand would drive molybdenum, nickel, cobalt and zinc prices up, discouraging mines with these by-products from cutting back. 



- The tightness of the scrap market may have been underestimated.  Lower industrial production generates less scrap and lower copper prices discourage scrap collection, this could result in the overestimation of refined production.  Conversely high prices encourage scrap collection and could allow higher copper production. 



- Project development could be even worse than expected, with higher than expected capital cost inflation, continued poor financing conditions, problems in mine equipment support industries and professional labour markets.  However, should the current lower capital cost

environment and shorter waits for longer lead time equipment allow more projects due to start up from 2011 onwards to come on-stream, we could be underestimating production. 



- A significant portion of major mining company debt is due to be re-financed in 2012-13. However, the future of the financial sector is still uncertain and credit markets may not have fully recovered by then.  If that is the case and a company cannot easily refinance then project development may be affected.  Project development by juniors would also be affected by continued tight credit conditions. 



- Labour issues associated with large job losses could affect production in the short term, whilst potentially tricky wage negotiations could occur from 2012 onwards, when the next major period of re-negotiations occurs.  This would be exacerbated if prices are higher than forecast. 



- Problems in Africa continue and the expected copper production growth in the region might not materialise, with low cobalt prices abetting such an outcome.  Long term infrastructure problems could get worse if countries effectively go bankrupt.  Civil unrest and civil war is extremely unlikely but could also drastically affect production. 



- Supply disruption due to ore grade and equipment failure has been a feature of the mining industry over the last few years.  Prolonged grade problems at Escondida or other major mines could lead to the overestimation of supply.  Similarly cost cutting could increase the chance of poor maintenance related failures and again lead to an overestimation of supply. A major earthquake in South America or Indonesia, or major floods in Australia or the copperbelt, would also cause temporary supply problems.  CRU, however, allows for a 6- 7.5% annual loss of production due to such factors in its forecast. 

#### **These are the main smelting/refining factors to be considered:** 



- We may have underestimated the effect of the tightness in the scrap market on refined production.  Our forecasts assume that, globally, production from scrap material will fall by 16% year on year in 2009 as lower levels of industrial activity reduce scrap generation and collection rates also fall as the lower copper price squeezes margins. However we may have underestimated the effect of the economic downturn on scrap generation, and/or lower prices on collection, and scrap availability could be tighter than anticipated.  In addition, if the downturn proves to be longer-lived than our forecasts assume, production from scrap could be lower than in future years.  Conversely, if prices persist at current levels, we may see more scrap become available, allowing higher levels of production from scrap. 



- Smelters are at risk from the global over supply of sulphuric acid; if they cannot ship their acid then they cannot continue to produce at current levels.  So far there have only been two cutbacks specifically as a result of the excess

supply of acid. Our forecasts include a market adjustment. However, some producers are being forced to store acid on ships at sea. Therefore, there is a risk that the impact of oversupply in the sulphuric acid market could well be greater than we have assumed. #### **The points apply to both mining and smelting/refining:** - Disruptions to mining and smelter output could occur in 2012 due to labour contracts coming due. With copper prices low, workers this year have less justification for making demands from their employers for large wage increases. However, by 2012 higher copper prices could give workers more fuel for their wage demands and we may see higher levels of disruption again in the final two years of the forecast. - Supply disruptions from equipment failure have been a feature of the supply side of the industry for the last three years. Reduced spending on equipment maintenance due to financial restrictions may well exacerbate this over the forecast period. If equipment is not maintained, or replaced when due, then it will be more vulnerable to failure. Reduced expenditure on mine development work may also have repercussions on future production levels.
